extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and delegates considering the structure and powers of the proposed U.S. government (readers of The Federalist)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and arguments for allocating treaty-making, appointment, and judicial powers in a republican constitution; explains what institutional arrangements promote energy, safety, responsibility, and stability. Focuses on who should make treaties, how appointments should be handled, and how a federal judicature should be constituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate allocation of the treaty-making power
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is to have power, 'by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur.' The power of making treaties partakes more of the legislative than the executive character, yet is properly a distinct department; the Executive is the most fit agent in foreign negotiations while the legislative body should participate because treaties operate as laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaties are contracts between sovereigns, not rules prescribed by sovereign to subject; therefore a joint arrangement (Executive negotiator + legislative participation) balances the need for executive qualities (secrecy, despatch, knowledge) with legislative safeguards (legal force of treaties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive as primary agent for foreign negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive possesses qualities indispensable in the management of foreign negotiations and is the most fit agent for those transactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualities highlighted: accurate and comprehensive knowledge of foreign politics, steady and systematic adherence to views, sensibility to national character, decision, secrecy, and despatch. These traits favor vesting negotiation power in the Executive rather than a large fluctuating assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative participation in treaty-making (Senate role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because treaties have the force of law and are of vast importance, the participation of the whole or a portion of the legislative body (the Senate) in making them is strongly urged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senate co-operation supplies additional security and legitimacy; a ministerial servant of the Senate would lack the confidence and respect of foreign powers compared to a constitutional representative. Joint possession of the power affords greater prospect of security than exclusive possession by either branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of the House of Representatives from treaty power
rubrics_metrics.description: The fluctuating and multitudinous composition of the House makes it unfit for the proper execution of the trust of treaty-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: House lacks secrecy, decision, and despatch; its size and variability would cause delays, expense, and complexity in progressive stages of treaty sanction, thereby making it unsuitable for foreign negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion requirement: two-thirds of senators PRESENT
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution requires two thirds of the senators present to concur in treaties, not two thirds of all members composing the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring a proportion of attending members avoids turning the requirement into practical unanimity due to absences; higher fixed proportions tend to embarrass government operations and render majority sense subject to minority. Making a proportion of present members incentivizes punctual attendance and reduces delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding supermajority/quorum rules that hinder government action
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions requiring more than a majority have a tendency to embarrass operations of government and subject the majority to the minority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive fixed-number thresholds (e.g., two thirds of whole membership) can amount in practice to unanimity and cause impotence, perplexity, and disorder (examples cited: Roman Tribuneship, Polish Diet, States-General). Prefer proportion-of-present rules to maintain activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of appointments: nomination by President with Senate advice and consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The President shall 'nominate, and, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, appoint' principal officers; Congress may vest appointment of inferior officers elsewhere. Nomination by the President plus Senate concurrence is presented as the best modification of appointment power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nomination concentrates responsibility, induces the President to investigate qualifications, and—combined with Senate consent—serves as a check against favoritism, state prejudice, family connections, and pursuit of popularity. The possibility of Senate rejection disciplines nominations and promotes care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer single accountable nominator over collective appointing bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: One man of discernment (the President) is better fitted to analyze and estimate peculiar qualities adapted to particular offices than a collective assembly of comparable discernment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single responsible nominator has fewer personal attachments, greater sense of duty and reputation, and less susceptibility to bargaining and compromise that obscure merit. Collective appointment risks party bargaining, compromises, and the rise of private or factional considerations over merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Senate concurrence to check executive favoritism
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate's concurrence acts as an excellent check upon a spirit of favoritism in the President and tends to prevent appointment of unfit characters due to state prejudice, family connection, personal attachment, or view to popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessity of concurrence makes nomination more carefully considered; the danger to the President’s reputation and political existence from evident favoritism deter improper selections. Senate approval thus contributes to stability of administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of opaque small councils of appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: Councils of appointment (small closed bodies) foster cabal, intrigue, lack of public accountability, opaque exercise of power, and frequent improper appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small secretive bodies are easy to manage or corrupt, encourage bargaining for places, produce monopolies of employment, reduce responsibility, and make it difficult for the public to attribute blame; they are therefore inferior to the proposed President + Senate model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate participation enhances stability of administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Senate consent is necessary to displace as well as to appoint; this prevents a change of Chief Magistrate from causing violent or general revolutions in public officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Senate has greater permanency, its role restrains new Presidents from wholesale removals and promotes steady administration; shared responsibility allocates public censure more transparently between Executive and Senate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional safeguards against executive influence on the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution provides guards: 'No senator or representative shall during the time for which he was elected be appointed to any civil office... which shall have been created, or the emoluments whereof shall have been increased, during such time; and no person, holding any office under the United States, shall be a member of either house during his continuance in office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions reduce temptations or opportunities for the Executive to influence legislative members via appointments, helping preserve Senate integrity and making wholesale corruption of the body impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency timeliness versus legislative sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: In urgent situations (rebels, invasions, restorations of tranquillity), delay in convening the legislature to obtain sanction may forfeit a 'golden opportunity'; discretionary emergency power for the President is questioned as possibly undelgatable or politically unwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness is critical—loss of a week, a day, an hour may be fatal. Nevertheless, granting a standing discretionary power to an elective magistrate is questionable both constitutionally and practically (temptation to abuse, appearance of impunity). The preference is for arrangements that allow prompt action without creating incentives to executive overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional design of the judiciary (objects to consider)
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner of constituting a federal judicature involves: 1) the mode of appointing the judges; 2) the tenure by which they are to hold their places; 3) the partition of the judiciary authority between different courts and their relations to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three objects frame evaluation of any scheme for a federal judicature. (The text indicates appointment mode follows the general appointment scheme; full guidance on tenure and partition to be examined.)
